lesson_scope: Composite areas formed from one curve integral and one straight-sided area, including add/subtract, chord, horizontal-line, tangent and below-axis cases.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: adding a curve area to an adjacent triangle area.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of adding a definite integral to an adjacent geometric triangle.

hints: Compute the area under the curve $y = 3x^2$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$ by evaluating $\int_0^2 3x^2 \, dx$.
Integrate: $\left[x^3\right]_0^2 = 2^3 - 0 = 8$.
Calculate the area of the right-angled triangle: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$.
Add the two non-overlapping areas together: $8 + 4 = 12$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Find the area under the curve $y = 3x^2$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = \int_0^2 3x^2 \, dx = \left[x^3\right]_0^2 = 2^3 - 0 = 8$$

Calculate the area of the adjacent right-angled triangle:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$$

Sum the two component areas:
$$\text{Total Area} = \text{Area}_{\text{curve}} + \text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = 8 + 4 = 12 \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Integrates $\int_0^2 3x^2 \, dx = \left[x^3\right]_0^2 = 8$ and finds triangle area $\frac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$.
Sums both components to obtain $12$ square units.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: subtracting a curve area from an outer triangle area.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of subtracting a curve integral from an outer geometric shape.

hints: Find the area of the outer triangle bounded by the axes and line from $(0, 4)$ to $(2, 0)$: $\text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$.
Find the area under the curve $y = x^2$ on $[0, 2]$: $\int_0^2 x^2 \, dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{8}{3}$.
Subtract the curve area from the triangle area: $4 - \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{12 - 8}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the area of the outer triangle bounded by the coordinate axes and the hypotenuse:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$$

Evaluate the area under the curve $y = x^2$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = \int_0^2 x^2 \, dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \frac{8}{3} - 0 = \frac{8}{3}$$

Subtract the area under the curve from the triangle area:
$$\text{Enclosed Area} = \text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} - \text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = 4 - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{4}{3} \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Finds triangle area $\frac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4$ and integrates $\int_0^2 x^2 \, dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \frac{8}{3}$.
Subtracts to obtain $4 - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$ square units.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: area between a parabola and a horizontal chord.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of integrating curve minus horizontal chord.

hints: Since both points $A(0, 3)$ and $B(2, 3)$ have $y = 3$, the chord $AB$ is the line $y = 3$ on the interval $[0, 2]$.
The curve lies above the chord on $(0, 2)$: form the vertical difference $(3 + 2x - x^2) - 3 = 2x - x^2$.
Integrate the difference: $\int_0^2 (2x - x^2) \, dx = \left[x^2 - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \left(4 - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) - 0 = \dfrac{4}{3}$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the equation of the chord $AB$:
Since $A(0, 3)$ and $B(2, 3)$ have identical $y$-coordinates, the chord is the horizontal line $y = 3$ for $x \in [0, 2]$.

Form the difference between the upper curve and the lower chord:
$$y_{\text{upper}} - y_{\text{lower}} = (3 + 2x - x^2) - 3 = 2x - x^2$$

Set up and evaluate the definite integral:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^2 (2x - x^2) \, dx = \left[x^2 - \frac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^2 = \left(2^2 - \frac{2^3}{3}\right) - 0 = 4 - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{4}{3} \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies chord $y = 3$ and forms $\int_0^2 (2x - x^2) \, dx = \left[x^2 - \frac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^2$.
Evaluates limits to obtain $\frac{4}{3}$ square units.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: area between a radical curve and a straight chord through origin.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of finding chord equation and integrating curve minus chord.

hints: Find the equation of the line chord passing through $(0, 0)$ and $(4, 4)$: gradient $m = \dfrac{4 - 0}{4 - 0} = 1$, so the chord is $y = x$.
The curve $y = 2\sqrt{x} = 2x^{1/2}$ lies above the chord on $(0, 4)$ (at $x = 1$, $2\sqrt{1} = 2 > 1$).
Set up the area integral with curve minus chord: $\int_0^4 (2x^{1/2} - x) \, dx$.
Integrate: $\left[\dfrac{4}{3}x^{3/2} - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\right]_0^4 = \left(\dfrac{4}{3}(8) - \dfrac{1}{2}(16)\right) - 0 = \dfrac{32}{3} - 8 = \dfrac{8}{3}$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Find the equation of the straight chord $PQ$:
$$\text{Gradient } m = \frac{4 - 0}{4 - 0} = 1 \implies y = x$$

Set up the area integral for the region between the upper radical curve and the lower chord on $[0, 4]$:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^4 (2x^{1/2} - x) \, dx$$

Integrate and evaluate at the limits:
$$= \left[\frac{4}{3}x^{3/2} - \frac{1}{2}x^2\right]_0^4 = \left(\frac{4}{3}(4^{3/2}) - \frac{1}{2}(4^2)\right) - 0 = \frac{32}{3} - 8 = \frac{8}{3} \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Finds chord line $y = x$ and integrates $\int_0^4 (2x^{1/2} - x) \, dx = \left[\frac{4}{3}x^{3/2} - \frac{1}{2}x^2\right]_0^4$.
Evaluates limits to obtain $\frac{32}{3} - 8 = \frac{8}{3}$ square units.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: combining reciprocal curve integral with a rectangle.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of integrating a negative power and adding an adjacent rectangle.

hints: Express $\dfrac{4}{x^2}$ with a negative index as $4x^{-2}$.
Integrate from $x = 1$ to $x = 2$: $\int_1^2 4x^{-2} \, dx = \left[-\dfrac{4}{x}\right]_1^2 = \left(-\dfrac{4}{2}\right) - \left(-\dfrac{4}{1}\right) = -2 + 4 = 2$.
Calculate the rectangle area: $\text{width} \times \text{height} = 3 \times 1 = 3$.
Sum the two areas: $2 + 3 = 5$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Find the area under the reciprocal curve $y = 4x^{-2}$ from $x = 1$ to $x = 2$:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = \int_1^2 4x^{-2} \, dx = \left[-\frac{4}{x}\right]_1^2 = \left(-\frac{4}{2}\right) - \left(-\frac{4}{1}\right) = -2 - (-4) = 2$$

Calculate the area of the adjoining rectangle:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{rectangle}} = \text{width} \times \text{height} = 3 \times 1 = 3$$

Add the two non-overlapping component areas:
$$\text{Total Area} = \text{Area}_{\text{curve}} + \text{Area}_{\text{rectangle}} = 2 + 3 = 5 \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Integrates $\int_1^2 4x^{-2} \, dx = \left[-\frac{4}{x}\right]_1^2 = 2$ and calculates rectangle area $3 \times 1 = 3$.
Sums both components to obtain $5$ square units.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: calculating total geometric area across an axis crossing point.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of splitting an integral at an axis crossing to find positive geometric area.

hints: Find the $x$-intercept on $[0, 3]$: $4 - x^2 = 0 \implies x = 2$.
For $x \in [0, 2]$, $y \ge 0$, so its area is $\int_0^2 (4 - x^2) \, dx = \left[4x - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = 8 - \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{16}{3}$.
For $x \in [2, 3]$, $y \le 0$, so its positive geometric area is $\int_2^3 (x^2 - 4) \, dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} - 4x\right]_2^3 = (9 - 12) - \left(\dfrac{8}{3} - 8\right) = \dfrac{7}{3}$.
Add the two positive regions: $\dfrac{16}{3} + \dfrac{7}{3} = \dfrac{23}{3}$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis on $[0, 3]$:
$$4 - x^2 = 0 \implies x = 2$$
On $[0, 2]$, the curve is above the $x$-axis ($y \ge 0$).
On $[2, 3]$, the curve is below the $x$-axis ($y \le 0$).

Calculate the positive area $A_1$ for the region above the axis on $[0, 2]$:
$$A_1 = \int_0^2 (4 - x^2) \, dx = \left[4x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = 8 - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{16}{3}$$

Calculate the positive area $A_2$ for the region below the axis on $[2, 3]$:
$$A_2 = \int_2^3 (x^2 - 4) \, dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - 4x\right]_2^3 = (9 - 12) - \left(\frac{8}{3} - 8\right) = -3 - \left(-\frac{16}{3}\right) = \frac{7}{3}$$

Sum the positive areas of both sections:
$$\text{Total Geometric Area} = A_1 + A_2 = \frac{16}{3} + \frac{7}{3} = \frac{23}{3} \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Splits at $x = 2$ and forms $\int_0^2 (4 - x^2) \, dx + \int_2^3 (x^2 - 4) \, dx$.
Evaluates both integrals: $\frac{16}{3} + \frac{7}{3} = \frac{23}{3}$ square units.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: The source supports comparing a straight-line boundary with a curve integral. This task replaces the source rectangle-minus-curve configuration with two intersecting algebraic graphs and a single upper-minus-lower integral.

closest_comparison.specific_configuration: Custom configuration: The curve $y = x^2$ and the line $y = 2x$ intersect at the origin and at a second point. Find the exact area enclosed by the curve and the line.
closest_comparison.operation_reasoning_chain: $x^2 = 2x$ gives $x(x - 2) = 0$, so the intersections have $x = 0$ and $x = 2$. For $0 \le x \le 2$, $2x - x^2 = x(2 - x) \ge 0$, so the line is above the curve. Area $= \int_0^2 (2x - x^2) \, dx = [x^2 - x^3/3]_0^2 = 4/3$ square units.
closest_comparison.material_difference: The source supports comparing a straight-line boundary with a curve integral. This task replaces the source rectangle-minus-curve configuration with two intersecting algebraic graphs and a single upper-minus-lower integral.

domain_and_existence_restrictions: $0 \le x \le 2$; $2x - x^2 = x(2 - x) \ge 0$ throughout the interval, so the line is the upper boundary.
hints: Find the intersection points by setting the line equation equal to the curve equation: $x^2 = 2x \implies x^2 - 2x = 0 \implies x(x - 2) = 0$.
Identify which graph is upper on the interval $(0, 2)$: test $x = 1$, where $y_{\text{line}} = 2(1) = 2$ and $y_{\text{curve}} = 1^2 = 1$, so the line lies above the curve.
Set up the area integral with upper line minus lower curve: $\int_0^2 (2x - x^2) \, dx$.
Integrate term-by-term: $\left[x^2 - \dfrac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^2 = \left(2^2 - \dfrac{2^3}{3}\right) - 0 = 4 - \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Find the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points:
$$x^2 = 2x \implies x^2 - 2x = 0 \implies x(x - 2) = 0 \implies x = 0, \quad x = 2$$

Determine which function is upper on the interval $[0, 2]$:
Testing $x = 1$: $y_{\text{line}} = 2(1) = 2$ and $y_{\text{curve}} = 1^2 = 1$.
Since $2 > 1$, the upper function is $y_{\text{upper}} = 2x$ and the lower function is $y_{\text{lower}} = x^2$.

Set up the area integral for the enclosed region:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^2 (2x - x^2) \, dx = \left[x^2 - \frac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^2$$

Substitute the limits to evaluate the exact area:
$$= \left(2^2 - \frac{2^3}{3}\right) - \left(0^2 - \frac{0^3}{3}\right) = 4 - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{4}{3} \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Solves $x^2 = 2x$ to obtain the intersection limits $x = 0$ and $x = 2$.
Forms $\int_0^2 (2x - x^2) \, dx$, with the line as the upper boundary.
Uses the antiderivative $\left[x^2 - \frac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^2$ and applies both limits.
Obtains the exact enclosed area $\frac{4}{3}$ square units.

closest_comparison.specific_configuration: Custom configuration: The line segment joining $(0, 6)$ to $(3, 0)$, the curve $y = \frac{1}{2}x(3 - x)$ and the $y$-axis enclose a region. Find the exact area of the region.
closest_comparison.operation_reasoning_chain: The triangle below the line segment has area $\frac{1}{2}(3)(6) = 9$. $\int_0^3 \frac{1}{2}x(3 - x) \, dx = [3x^2/4 - x^3/6]_0^3 = 9/4$. Enclosed area is $9 - 9/4 = 27/4$ square units.
closest_comparison.material_difference: The source supports combining a curve integral with a triangle. Here the curve lies inside one triangle over a shared interval, so the learner subtracts rather than adding two adjacent regions.

domain_and_existence_restrictions: $0 \le x \le 3$; the line is $y = 6 - 2x$, and $(6 - 2x) - \frac{1}{2}x(3 - x) = \frac{1}{2}(x - 3)(x - 4) \ge 0$ throughout the interval.
hints: The region lies between the line segment from $(0, 6)$ to $(3, 0)$ and the curve $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x(3 - x)$ above the $x$-axis from $x = 0$ to $x = 3$.

Calculate the area of the large right-angled triangle formed by the line segment and the axes: $\text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2}(3)(6) = 9$.
Find the area under the curve from $x = 0$ to $x = 3$ by integrating: $\int_0^3 \left(\dfrac{3}{2}x - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\right) \, dx = \left[\dfrac{3}{4}x^2 - \dfrac{1}{6}x^3\right]_0^3$.
Subtract the curve area from the triangle area: $9 - \left(\dfrac{27}{4} - \dfrac{27}{6}\right) = 9 - \dfrac{9}{4} = \dfrac{27}{4}$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Find the area of the right-angled triangle bounded by the line segment and the coordinate axes:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2}(3)(6) = 9$$

Expand and integrate the curve $y = \frac{1}{2}x(3 - x) = \frac{3}{2}x - \frac{1}{2}x^2$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 3$:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = \int_0^3 \left(\frac{3}{2}x - \frac{1}{2}x^2\right) \, dx = \left[\frac{3}{4}x^2 - \frac{1}{6}x^3\right]_0^3$$

Evaluate the curve area at the limits $x = 3$ and $x = 0$:
$$= \left(\frac{3(3)^2}{4} - \frac{3^3}{6}\right) - 0 = \frac{27}{4} - \frac{27}{6} = \frac{81 - 54}{12} = \frac{27}{12} = \frac{9}{4}$$

Subtract the area under the curve from the triangle area to obtain the enclosed region:
$$\text{Enclosed Area} = \text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} - \text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = 9 - \frac{9}{4} = \frac{36 - 9}{4} = \frac{27}{4} \text{ square units}$$

closest_comparison.specific_configuration: Custom configuration: The points $P(1, 5)$ and $Q(5, 5)$ lie on the curve $y = 6x - x^2$. Find the exact area enclosed by the curve and the chord $PQ$.
closest_comparison.operation_reasoning_chain: The chord through $P$ and $Q$ is $y = 5$. The curve lies above it, so area $= \int_1^5 (6x - x^2 - 5) \, dx = [3x^2 - x^3/3 - 5x]_1^5 = 32/3$ square units.
closest_comparison.material_difference: The source supports curve-minus-chord area. Here the chord is horizontal, the curve is polynomial, the coordinates and limits differ, and the answer is exact rather than decimal.

domain_and_existence_restrictions: $1 \le x \le 5$; $6x - x^2 - 5 = 4 - (x - 3)^2 \ge 0$ on the interval, so the curve is the upper boundary.
hints: Notice that both points $P(1, 5)$ and $Q(5, 5)$ have the same $y$-coordinate, so the chord $PQ$ is the horizontal line $y = 5$.
On the interval $(1, 5)$, the curve lies above the chord (at the vertex $x = 3$, $y_{\text{curve}} = 6(3) - 9 = 9 > 5$), so $y_{\text{upper}} = 6x - x^2$ and $y_{\text{lower}} = 5$.
Form the difference $y_{\text{upper}} - y_{\text{lower}} = (6x - x^2) - 5 = 6x - x^2 - 5$ and set up the integral $\int_1^5 (6x - x^2 - 5) \, dx$.

Integrate: $\left[3x^2 - \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 - 5x\right]_1^5 = \left(75 - \dfrac{125}{3} - 25\right) - \left(3 - \dfrac{1}{3} - 5\right) = \left(50 - \dfrac{125}{3}\right) - \left(-2 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{25}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right) = \dfrac{32}{3}$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the equation of the chord $PQ$:
Since $P(1, 5)$ and $Q(5, 5)$ share the $y$-coordinate $5$, the chord is the horizontal line $y = 5$ spanning $x \in [1, 5]$.

Determine the upper function on $[1, 5]$:
At the vertex $x = 3$, $y_{\text{curve}} = 6(3) - 3^2 = 9 > 5$, so $y_{\text{upper}} = 6x - x^2$ and $y_{\text{lower}} = 5$.

Set up the area integral with upper curve minus lower chord:
$$\text{Area} = \int_1^5 \left((6x - x^2) - 5\right) \, dx = \int_1^5 (6x - x^2 - 5) \, dx$$

Integrate and substitute the limits:
$$= \left[3x^2 - \frac{1}{3}x^3 - 5x\right]_1^5$$
$$\text{At } x = 5: \quad 3(25) - \frac{125}{3} - 5(5) = 75 - \frac{125}{3} - 25 = 50 - \frac{125}{3} = \frac{25}{3}$$
$$\text{At } x = 1: \quad 3(1) - \frac{1}{3} - 5(1) = 3 - \frac{1}{3} - 5 = -2 - \frac{1}{3} = -\frac{7}{3}$$
$$\text{Area} = \frac{25}{3} - \left(-\frac{7}{3}\right) = \frac{32}{3} \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies the chord as $y = 5$ over $1 \le x \le 5$.

Applies both limits to a correct antiderivative $\left[3x^2 - \frac{1}{3}x^3 - 5x\right]_1^5$.
Obtains the exact enclosed area $\frac{32}{3}$ square units.

closest_comparison.specific_configuration: Custom configuration: A composite region consists of the area under $y = \sqrt{x + 1}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 3$, together with a rectangle of width $2$ and height $2$ placed next to that curved part. Find the exact total area.
closest_comparison.operation_reasoning_chain: $\int_0^3 \sqrt{x + 1} \, dx = [\frac{2}{3}(x + 1)^{3/2}]_0^3 = \frac{2}{3}(8 - 1) = 14/3$. Rectangle area is $2 \times 2 = 4$. Total is $14/3 + 4 = 26/3$ square units.

domain_and_existence_restrictions: The curve requires $x \ge -1$; the curved part uses $0 \le x \le 3$, and the separate rectangle has positive dimensions $2$ by $2$.
hints: Break the composite region into two separate parts: the area under the curve $y = (x + 1)^{1/2}$ on $[0, 3]$, and the area of the rectangle.
Use the linear reverse chain rule to integrate $(x + 1)^{1/2}$: $\int (x + 1)^{1/2} \, dx = \dfrac{(x + 1)^{3/2}}{3/2} = \dfrac{2}{3}(x + 1)^{3/2}$.
Add the rectangle's area: $\text{Total Area} = \dfrac{14}{3} + (2 \times 2) = \dfrac{14}{3} + 4 = \dfrac{26}{3}$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Set up the integral for the area under the curved portion $y = \sqrt{x + 1} = (x + 1)^{1/2}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 3$:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = \int_0^3 (x + 1)^{1/2} \, dx$$

Integrate using the reverse chain rule:
$$= \left[\frac{(x + 1)^{3/2}}{3/2}\right]_0^3 = \left[\frac{2}{3}(x + 1)^{3/2}\right]_0^3$$

Calculate the rectangle area and add the two non-overlapping components:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{rectangle}} = 2 \times 2 = 4$$
$$\text{Total Area} = \text{Area}_{\text{curve}} + \text{Area}_{\text{rectangle}} = \frac{14}{3} + 4 = \frac{14 + 12}{3} = \frac{26}{3} \text{ square units}$$

closest_comparison.specific_configuration: Custom configuration: The curve $y = x^2 - 1$ is considered from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$. A separate triangle has base $2$ units and perpendicular height $3$ units. Find the total of the geometric area between the curve and the $x$-axis and the area of the triangle.
closest_comparison.operation_reasoning_chain: $x^2 - 1 = 0$ gives $x = 1$. $\int_0^1 (1 - x^2) \, dx = 2/3$ and $\int_1^2 (x^2 - 1) \, dx = 4/3$, so curve-axis area is $2$. Triangle area is $\frac{1}{2}(2)(3) = 3$. Total is $2 + 3 = 5$ square units.
closest_comparison.material_difference: The source supports combining positive geometric curve area with a triangle. This task introduces an internal axis crossing and requires two signed-area pieces rather than taking one integral's magnitude.

domain_and_existence_restrictions: $0 \le x \le 2$; the curve is below the axis on $[0, 1]$ and above it on $[1, 2]$, and the separate triangle has positive base $2$ and height $3$.
hints: Find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis: $x^2 - 1 = 0 \implies x = 1$ on the interval $[0, 2]$.

Notice that on $[0, 1]$, $y = x^2 - 1 \le 0$ (below the axis), so its positive geometric area is $\int_0^1 (1 - x^2) \, dx$. On $[1, 2]$, $y \ge 0$ (above the axis), so its area is $\int_1^2 (x^2 - 1) \, dx$.

Evaluate each piece: $\left[x - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, and $\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_1^2 = \left(\dfrac{8}{3} - 2\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{3} - 1\right) = \dfrac{2}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{4}{3}$. Sum for curve area $= \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} = 2$.
Calculate the triangle area: $\dfrac{1}{2}(2)(3) = 3$, and add them together: $2 + 3 = 5$ square units.

walkthrough.text:
Find the $x$-intercept to split the geometric area:
$$x^2 - 1 = 0 \implies x = 1$$
On $[0, 1]$, $x^2 - 1 \le 0$ (region lies below the $x$-axis).
On $[1, 2]$, $x^2 - 1 \ge 0$ (region lies above the $x$-axis).

Set up and evaluate the two positive curve-axis area integrals:
$$A_1 = \int_0^1 (1 - x^2) \, dx = \left[x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = 1 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3}$$
$$A_2 = \int_1^2 (x^2 - 1) \, dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_1^2 = \left(\frac{8}{3} - 2\right) - \left(\frac{1}{3} - 1\right) = \frac{2}{3} - \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = \frac{4}{3}$$
$$\text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = A_1 + A_2 = \frac{2}{3} + \frac{4}{3} = 2$$

Calculate the area of the separate triangle:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2}(2)(3) = 3$$

Sum the curve-axis geometric area and triangle area:
$$\text{Total Area} = \text{Area}_{\text{curve}} + \text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = 2 + 3 = 5 \text{ square units}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies the sign change at $x = 1$ and splits the curve-axis area there.
Evaluates the combined curve-axis geometric area as $2$.
Finds the triangle area $\frac{1}{2}(2)(3) = 3$.
Adds the positive areas to obtain $5$ square units.

closest_comparison.specific_configuration: Custom configuration: The points $P(0, 4)$ and $Q(8, 12)$ lie on the curve $y = 4\sqrt{x + 1}$. The chord $PQ$ and the curve enclose a region. Find the exact fraction of the area under the curve from $x = 0$ to $x = 8$ that lies between the curve and the chord.
closest_comparison.operation_reasoning_chain: $\int_0^8 4\sqrt{x + 1} \, dx = [\frac{8}{3}(x + 1)^{3/2}]_0^8 = 208/3$. Trapezium under $PQ$ has parallel sides $4$ and $12$, width $8$, area $64$. Enclosed area is $208/3 - 64 = 16/3$. As fraction: $(16/3)/(208/3) = 1/13$.
closest_comparison.material_difference: The source supports comparing a curve integral with a chord trapezium. This task changes the curve and endpoints and, materially, asks for the enclosed region as a fraction of the whole curve area rather than the enclosed area itself.

domain_and_existence_restrictions: The root curve requires $x \ge -1$; the region uses $0 \le x \le 8$, where concavity places the curve on or above chord $PQ$.
hints: First find the total area under the curve $y = 4(x + 1)^{1/2}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 8$ by integrating: $\int_0^8 4(x + 1)^{1/2} \, dx = \left[\dfrac{8}{3}(x + 1)^{3/2}\right]_0^8$.

Find the area under the chord $PQ$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 8$: this forms a trapezium with parallel vertical heights $y_P = 4$ and $y_Q = 12$ and width $8$: $\text{Area}_{\text{trapezium}} = \dfrac{1}{2}(4 + 12)(8) = 64$.
Calculate the enclosed area: $\dfrac{208}{3} - 64 = \dfrac{208 - 192}{3} = \dfrac{16}{3}$. Then find the fraction of the total curve area: $\dfrac{16/3}{208/3} = \dfrac{16}{208} = \dfrac{1}{13}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the total area under the curve $y = 4\sqrt{x + 1} = 4(x + 1)^{1/2}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 8$:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = \int_0^8 4(x + 1)^{1/2} \, dx = \left[\frac{4(x + 1)^{3/2}}{3/2}\right]_0^8 = \left[\frac{8}{3}(x + 1)^{3/2}\right]_0^8$$

Find the area under the chord $PQ$ as a trapezium with parallel vertical sides $y = 4$ and $y = 12$ across width $8$:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{trapezium}} = \frac{1}{2}(y_P + y_Q)(x_Q - x_P) = \frac{1}{2}(4 + 12)(8 - 0) = \frac{1}{2}(16)(8) = 64$$

Find the enclosed area between curve and chord, and compute the fraction of the total curve area:
$$\text{Enclosed Area} = \text{Area}_{\text{curve}} - \text{Area}_{\text{trapezium}} = \frac{208}{3} - 64 = \frac{208 - 192}{3} = \frac{16}{3}$$
$$\text{Required Fraction} = \frac{\text{Enclosed Area}}{\text{Area}_{\text{curve}}} = \frac{16/3}{208/3} = \frac{16}{208} = \frac{1}{13}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Forms $\int_0^8 4\sqrt{x + 1} \, dx$.
Uses the correct antiderivative $\left[\frac{8}{3}(x + 1)^{3/2}\right]_0^8$.
Applies both limits to obtain the area under the curve $\frac{208}{3}$.
Finds the trapezium under chord $PQ$ has area $\frac{1}{2}(4 + 12)(8) = 64$.
Finds the between-boundaries area $\frac{208}{3} - 64 = \frac{16}{3}$.
Divides by the full curve area to obtain the fraction $\frac{16/3}{208/3} = \frac{1}{13}$.

closest_comparison.specific_configuration: Custom configuration: A composite region consists of the area under the curve $y = 3\sqrt{x}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 4$, together with the triangle under the line segment joining $P(4, 6)$ to $Q(k, 0)$, where $k > 4$. Given that the total area is $28$, find the exact value of $k$.
closest_comparison.material_difference: The source adds a curve area and a triangle to obtain a total area. This task fixes the curve interval, parameterises a separate triangle endpoint and asks for that boundary coordinate from a given total, materially changing the requested result and dependency structure.

domain_and_existence_restrictions: $0 \le x \le 4$ lies in the root domain; $k > 4$ ensures the triangle has positive base $k - 4$ and height $6$.
hints: First evaluate the fixed area under the curve $y = 3x^{1/2}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 4$: $\int_0^4 3x^{1/2} \, dx = \left[2x^{3/2}\right]_0^4 = 2(4^{3/2}) - 0 = 2(8) = 16$.
Next express the area of the right-angled triangle under $PQ$: the base along the $x$-axis from $x = 4$ to $x = k$ has length $k - 4$, and the perpendicular vertical height is $y_P = 6$.
Form the triangle area: $\text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2}(k - 4)(6) = 3(k - 4)$.
Set the sum of the curved area and triangle area equal to $28$: $16 + 3(k - 4) = 28 \implies 3(k - 4) = 12 \implies k - 4 = 4 \implies k = 8$.

walkthrough.text:
Find the area under the curve $y = 3\sqrt{x} = 3x^{1/2}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 4$:
$$\text{Area}_{\text{curve}} = \int_0^4 3x^{1/2} \, dx = \left[\frac{3x^{3/2}}{3/2}\right]_0^4 = \left[2x^{3/2}\right]_0^4 = 2(4^{3/2}) - 0 = 2(8) = 16$$

Express the area of the triangle under the segment from $P(4, 6)$ to $Q(k, 0)$:
$$\text{Base} = k - 4, \quad \text{Height} = 6$$
$$\text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = \frac{1}{2} \times (k - 4) \times 6 = 3(k - 4)$$

Set up the total area equation:
$$\text{Total Area} = \text{Area}_{\text{curve}} + \text{Area}_{\text{triangle}} = 28$$
$$16 + 3(k - 4) = 28$$

Solve for $k$:
$$3(k - 4) = 28 - 16 = 12$$
$$k - 4 = 4 \implies k = 8$$
Since $k = 8 > 4$, this gives the valid boundary coordinate.

Forms the total-area equation $16 + 3(k - 4) = 28$.
Solves to obtain $3(k - 4) = 12$.
Concludes $k = 8$, consistent with $k > 4$.
